approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Provide them with a variety of counters (e.g. cubes and beans) they can use to represent the coloured pencils in each pot. Show students Master 1. Ask them if they are able to show the data from the tally chart using the counters. Tell them your friend said she used one counter to represent each item on the tally chart. Is this possible? In what ways might we show that we are counting three different items? Can we use different-coloured counters? Can we arrange them in a graph or label them?
Allow students to arrange the data in different ways, prompting them to consider alternatives. Focusing on the examples in Master, prompt them to construct horizontal and vertical graphs as well. Tell the class your other friend said he could use 5 counters to represent the blue pencils. Is this possible? If 5 counters are used to represent the blue pencils, how many counters should be used for the red and green pencils? Can this be presented in a graph? Get them to draw the graph using this scale of 2.
During Guided Practice, students are using data presented in a graph to complete a table and then draw another picture graph with a scale of 2.

objective: interpret and present data using bar charts.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them questions about the graph, such as what each red cube represents and the number of each coloured pencils. Then ask students if they have heard of other types of graphs. Tell them that there are other types we can use to present data, such as the number of pencils.
Show students the bar graph in Master and ask them if they can see any similarities between the picture graph and the bar graph. What are the differences? Lead them to see that there are numbers shown on the line that reads 'number of pencils'. Introduce the word 'scale' to students. Tell them that in a bar graph we don't need to count the number as we would in the picture graph; instead we can tell the number by reading the 'scale'. Then proceed to show students how to read the 'scale' for each of the bars: 10 blue pencils, 4 red pencils and 8 green pencils.
Ask students which is the largest group of coloured pencils and which is the smallest. Can we find how many more the largest group have by looking at the graph? Show the class how to read the 'difference' by using the bar graph. Then ask them to show how many more blue pencils there are than red pencils.
During Guided Practice, students are interpreting information from a bar graph and answering related questions.
formative_assessment:
use the term 'bar graph'.
Students can differentiate between a picture graph and a bar graph.
Students know what the scale is on a bar graph.
Students can read a bar graph and answer questions related to it.

objective: interpret and present data using bar charts.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them what information they can learn from the bar graph. Tell them your friend knows which drink is the most popular and least popular. Is this true? Does the graph show this kind of information? Tell students you think it only shows how many drinks are sold. Allow them time to discuss what the graphs are showing.
Then ask students to work in groups of 4 to create 3 questions using the bar graph. Gather all the questions created and ask them to answer the questions. Go through the questions in Master. Did students create similar questions? Show them how to use the data from the graph to answer the questions.
During Guided Practice, students are answering questions about a bar graph that is horizontally represented. Ask them how this bar graph is different from the one in the Explore task. Guide them to see that the graphs are essentially the same, only presented in a different orientation.
formative_assessment:
use the term 'bar graph'.
Students know what the scale is on the bar graph.
Students can read a bar graph and answer questions related to it.
Students can read a bar graph presented horizontally.

objective: interpret and present data using scaled bar charts.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and allow them time to look at the information presented. Ask them how children walked to school. How about taking the bus? Then ask them if they can tell you how many children cycled to school.
Prompt students to look at the scale of the graph and discuss what might have been the issue. It is important that they are able to determine the scale of a graph, so spend time focusing on how to read the scale with them. Draw their attention to the small markings between the numbers. What does each marking represent? Guide students to count on to determine what each marking represents. Help them to use the knowledge gained from previous lessons on reading measurements from different scales.
Show students how to determine the number of children who cycled to school by drawing a dotted line down from the cycle bar to the scale. Guide students to count on from 10, and then count backwards from 15. Ask them to use the same method to find the number children who took the car to school. Ask students to work in groups of 4 to create 3 more questions using the bar graph, and then get them to exchange their questions with another group and find the answers.
During Guided Practice, students are reading the information from a bar graph with a scale of 10.

Students can determine the scale on the bar graph.

objective: interpret and present data using scaled bar charts.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with an enlarged version of the graph from the Explore task. Ask them to describe the information presented. Remind them to determine the scale used for this bar graph. Give them time to read the graph and then give you some responses. Write their descriptions on the board.
Ask students to look at Charles' statement. Is it correct? Ask them to use the bar graph to check his statement. Then ask students to use the bar graph to gather more information they could use to make their own statements.
During Guided Practice, students are reading a horizontal bar graph based on the number of children who attended an after-school activity over five days.
